canonical_question: What are the specific size distributions of the elemental precursor powders used to synthesize the CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy?

question_variants.question: Why were the raw powder particles sized so differently across elements, particularly the 2-5 µm Ti versus the 45-60 µm Co/Ni?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The raw powder particle sizes differ across elements as listed in the experimental details: Co and Ni were 45-60 µm, Cr was 10-30 µm, Fe was 10-20 µm, and Ti was 2-5 µm.

answers.answer: These elemental powders included cobalt (99.8% purity, particle ranging from 45 µm to 60 µm), chromium (99.7% purity, particle ranging from 10 µm to 30 µm), iron (99.96% purity, particle ranging from 10 µm to 20 µm), nickel (99.5% purity, particle ranging from 45 µm to 60 µm), and titanium (99.95% purity, particle ranging from 2 µm to 5 µm).
answers.measurement_outcome: Particle sizes: Co 45-60 µm, Cr 10-30 µm, Fe 10-20 µm, Ni 45-60 µm, Ti 2-5 µm
evidence_spans: High–entropy alloy powders composed of CoCrFeNiTi were prepared using a mechanical alloying process through high–energy ball milling (HEBM) under argon atmosphere.

These elemental powders included cobalt (99.8% purity, particle ranging from 45 µm to 60 µm), chromium (99.7% purity, particle ranging from 10 µm to 30 µm), iron (99.96% purity, particle ranging from 10 µm to 20 µm), nickel (99.5% purity, particle ranging from 45 µm to 60 µm), and titanium (99.95% purity, particle ranging from 2 µm to 5 µm).
The milling process was conducted using a planetary ball mill model QM–1SP4, utilizing a stainless steel cylindrical vessel and balls with diameters between 5 mm and 10 mm.

cross_paper_synthesis.consensus: There is a single reported set of specifications for the raw elemental powders in this context, showing a deliberate disparity in particle sizes across the different elements.
cross_paper_synthesis.different_approaches: The provided source (PMC12298864) details a specific material specification where larger particles are selected for the transition metals (Co, Ni) while finer particles are used for Titanium, likely to optimize mixing kinetics or reaction stoichiometry during the subsequent processing.
cross_paper_synthesis.condition_dependencies: The reported sizes are strictly for the 'as-received' elemental powders before any mechanical alloying or heat treatment. The values do not apply to the final alloyed powder or consolidated material.
cross_paper_synthesis.contradictions: No contradictions exist within the provided dataset, as only one paper's data is available for comparison.
cross_paper_synthesis.evidence_strength: High for the specific sample described, as the values are direct observations of material specifications rather than derived estimates.
cross_paper_synthesis.unresolved_gap: The rationale for selecting such a wide range of initial particle sizes (from 2-5 µm to 45-60 µm) is not explicitly explained, nor is there data on how these initial disparities evolve during the mechanical alloying process.
cross_paper_synthesis.candidate_hypothesis: The selection of 2-5 µm Ti particles alongside 45-60 µm Co/Ni particles is intended to increase the specific surface area of Titanium, potentially compensating for its lower diffusion rate or ensuring complete reaction despite the size disparity.
cross_paper_synthesis.discriminating_experiment: Compare the homogeneity and final phase distribution of alloys synthesized using uniform-sized powders (e.g., all 10-20 µm) versus the reported size-differentiated batch to quantify the effect of initial size disparity on the final microstructure.
